title: Bidirectional BFS in Dublin: Faster Pathfinding!
description: Watch Bidirectional BFS sweep outward from start and goal on a real street-map grid, meeting in the middle to cut search work. This visualization shows how two coordinated BFS frontiers reduce runtime compared to one-way BFS.
ig_caption:
🚦🌍 **Bidirectional BFS** is like asking two teams to explore a city from both ends—then shaking hands at the shortest meeting point. 

🧠 **How it works (deep technical):** we run **BFS simultaneously** from the **start node** and the **goal node**, expanding level-by-level so the first time the frontiers intersect, we reconstruct an **optimal shortest path** (in unweighted graphs). This turns the search from exploring a big single radius into exploring two smaller radii—often shrinking the visited space dramatically. 

🗺️ **Graph theory on real streets:** model Dublin’s street network as a graph where **intersections = nodes** and **road segments = edges**. On that graph, each BFS frontier maintains a queue of nodes at increasing distance, while a hash/parent map lets us quickly detect the meeting node and stitch paths together. 

✅ Want me to visualize another route (park-to-landmark, shortest time, or least turns)? Comment your start & end points! 👍
fb_caption:
In Dublin (Smithfield), we visualize **Bidirectional BFS** as a graph search strategy: instead of exploring from start all the way to the goal, we search **from both ends** and stop as soon as the two BFS frontiers meet. 📍

On real street maps, this means treating intersections as nodes and roads as edges—then using BFS’s guarantee of shortest paths in unweighted graphs to efficiently reconstruct the optimal route.
